source_read: PDF (scan), pp. 347-360, all pages read on the rendered page at 150 dpi; Tables 1-9 and the passages on pp. 349 and 357 checked at 300 dpi; text layer used only to locate passages

claims.overstatement: Numbers are right, but four points of wording go beyond this source or leave out its qualifiers. (1) 'so the design seldom separates alcohol from belief' reports half of the authors' argument: they say the manipulation was not unconfounded and alcohol almost always alters expectancy (pp. 357-358), but also that for no dependent variable did alcohol and expectancy both have significant effects, so the alcohol effects cannot be attributed to expectancy (p. 358). The claim should add that. (2) 'at the low doses these designs allow' has no basis in this paper: no doses were extracted or reported; the only mention of dose is others' claim about the dose levels used in laboratory research (p. 348). (3) The pooled drinking category is 'reported desire or actual consumption' in studies the authors describe as of alcoholics (p. 354): one of the three (Maisto et al., 1977, a reanalysis of Engle & Williams, 1972) concerns desire, so 'increased how much men drank in a short taste test' rests on Marlatt et al. and not on the pooled 0.52. (4) 'The meta-analysis averages amount drunk with sip counts' is an inference: the paper says only that several indicators of one variable were averaged within a study (p. 349). My reconstruction from Marlatt's printed F values and means reproduces both printed values only if three measures were averaged, total amount (1.13), sip count (-0.03) and amount per sip (0.86), mean 0.66; for alcohol -0.18, -0.50 and +0.16, mean -0.17. Amount and sips alone give 0.55 and -0.34. The conclusion that 0.66 understates the effect on amount (about 1.1) stands. The expectancy effects on sexual arousal, mood, bodily arousal and aggression were significantly heterogeneous, which the claim does not say.
claims.note: All figures checked at 300 dpi. 36 experiments in 34 articles, published before September 1985 (earliest 1972). 144 main effects each of alcohol and expectancy; 50 and 65 of undetermined size set to zero = 34.7% and 45.1% (recomputed; claim's 'about 35% to 45%' matches). The authors call this conservative and say that leaving those effects out never changed a conclusion about whether an effect existed (p. 349). Weighting: the Z is described as an unweighted Stouffer Z, and every printed mean g equals the simple mean of the printed study values with 'ns' as zero (recomputed for Tables 2-9, differences only from rounding, e.g. Table 2 alcohol 0.536 vs 0.5344). No table or text gives confidence intervals. No doses, sample sizes or participant descriptions are given for any study (the Appendix lists citations only); sex appears in one post hoc contrast on physiological arousal (p. 352). Category means match the claim: expectancy on sexual arousal 0.306 (Z = 2.861, p < .01, 9 studies), drinking 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01; 0.66, 0.52, 0.39), information processing -0.002, physical sensations 0.0450, motor 0.1230, mood 0.061, physiological arousal 0.046, aggression -0.131 (Z = -1.194); alcohol on information processing 0.5344 (Z = 3.618, p < .001, 5 studies), motor 0.6360 (Z = 3.725, p < .001, 3 studies), physical sensations 0.6440 (Z = 4.549, p < .001), mood 0.209 (Z = 3.026, p < .01), drinking -0.040, sexual arousal -0.017, aggression 0.255 (Z = 1.764, p < .10), physiological arousal -0.225 (Z = -1.193; a positive g there means decreased arousal). Manipulation check: 18 of 20 (90%) studies that did not first ask which drink was received found alcohol effects on the check, against 1 of 12 (8%) that asked first; 59% overall. Also relevant to bias: only 7 of 36 studies kept the experimenter blind to the expectancy condition (p. 355).

anchors.locator: Sample of Studies (right column, 1st paragraph); footnote 2
anchors.extracted: Balanced-placebo studies (randomized factorial crossing of alcohol vs placebo beverage with told alcohol vs told placebo) published before September 1985: 34 articles in eight journals, 36 experiments, earliest 1972. Studies manipulating expected effects or beverage type were excluded.

anchors.locator: Data Extracted From Each Study (p. 348 right column; p. 349 left column, 1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Variables of primary interest to the investigators only; 144 main effects of alcohol and 144 of expectancy, each as g = difference of marginal means over pooled SD and as z from the one-tailed p. After writing to authors, 50 alcohol and 65 expectancy effects remained of undetermined size and were set to zero (34.7% and 45.1%, editors' calculation); the authors call this conservative and report that excluding them never changed a conclusion on whether an effect existed.

Eleven dependent measures; effects signed by the predicted direction; several indicators of one variable averaged within a study; tables give mean g, an unweighted Stouffer Z and a heterogeneity chi-square, no intervals. Printed means equal simple means of the study values with 'ns' as zero (editors' check, Tables 2-9).

The only reference to dose is others' claim that expectancy outweighs alcohol at the dosage levels used in laboratory research (Wilson, 1977); no dose, sample size or participant data are extracted anywhere in the paper.
5 studies. Alcohol mean g 0.5344 (Z = 3.618, p < .001; heterogeneity chi-square(4) = 4.69); expectancy -0.002 (Z = -0.004; 0.79). Positive g = impairment. The text section calls these memory studies.

Physical sensations, 3 studies: alcohol 0.6440 (Z = 4.549, p < .001), expectancy 0.0450 (Z = 0.305). Mood, 14 studies: alcohol 0.209 (Z = 3.026, p < .01; chi-square(13) = 12.31), expectancy 0.061 (Z = 1.084; chi-square(13) = 22.38, p < .05).

8 studies: alcohol -0.225 (Z = -1.193; chi-square(7) = 46.48, p < .001; positive g = decreased arousal), 0.10 (Z = 0.91) without Briddell et al. 1978; expectancy 0.046 (Z = 0.333; chi-square(7) = 16.77, p < .05). Expectancy improved mood more in a humorous than a neutral setting (g 0.67 vs 0.00, Z = 2.89, p < .01; post hoc).

anchors.extracted: Motor, 3 studies: alcohol 0.6360 (Z = 3.725, p < .001; chi-square(2) = 6.90, p < .05; one study ns), expectancy 0.1230 (Z = 0.645). Sexual arousal, 9 studies: expectancy 0.306 (Z = 2.861, p < .01; chi-square(8) = 20.64, p < .01; study values -0.25 to 1.21), alcohol -0.017 (Z = -0.056; positive g = reduced arousal); expectancy effects similar on physiological and self-report measures (0.41 vs 0.33).
7 experiments: expectancy -0.131 (Z = -1.194; chi-square(6) = 18.40, p < .01), alcohol 0.255 (Z = 1.764, p < .10; chi-square(6) = 12.88, p < .05).

anchors.locator: p. 354 left column, Alcohol, expectancy, and alcohol consumption (last two paragraphs); p. 355 Table 9
anchors.extracted: Three studies of reported desire or actual drinking 'among alcoholics' (Berg et al., 1981; Maisto et al., 1977, a reanalysis of Engle & Williams, 1972; Marlatt et al., 1973). Expectancy g 0.66, 0.52, 0.39, mean 0.523 (Z = 2.870, p < .01; chi-square(2) = 0.32); alcohol -0.17, ns, 0.05, mean -0.040 (Z = -0.315).

anchors.locator: Utility of the Balanced-Placebo Design (right column, 2nd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Of studies with an expectancy manipulation check, 59% found significant alcohol effects on it: 1 of 12 (8%) that first asked which drink was consumed, 18 of 20 (90%) that did not. The authors conclude alcohol almost always alters expectancy and that checks reflect it unless demand is introduced.

anchors.locator: Success of the balanced-placebo design (left column, 3rd paragraph)
anchors.extracted: The design did not give an unconfounded manipulation, but for no dependent variable did alcohol and expectancy both have significant effects, so the authors conclude the alcohol effects cannot be attributed to expectancy.

anchors.locator: Other Issues: The Use of Blind Techniques
anchors.extracted: Only 7 of 36 studies kept the experimenter blind to the expectancy condition; mean effects did not differ by blindness (t < 1.00) but varied more when the experimenter was not blind (alcohol F = 3.76, p < .01; expectancy on nonsocial behaviours F = 5.07, p < .03).

key_findings.correction: Appendix count checked: 34 articles, earliest Marlatt et al. (1973), as the note says.

My blind reconstruction gives the same three-measure average (expectancy 1.134, -0.029, 0.862, mean 0.656; alcohol -0.177, -0.501, +0.163, mean -0.171); amount and sips alone would give 0.55 and -0.34.

Numbers and location confirmed. The authors state the consequence conditionally (if the design fails to provide such a condition, it cannot answer Marlatt and Rohsenow's question, p. 357). On p. 358 they add that alcohol and expectancy never both had significant effects on the same measure, so the alcohol effects cannot be attributed to expectancy (see missed).

reporting_issues.note: Checked against Table 7 (p. 353), Table 8 (p. 354), the text citations on pp. 353-354 and the Appendix (p. 359).
I also checked that each printed mean g equals the simple mean of the printed study values with 'ns' as zero (Tables 2-9).

The reconstruction is confirmed independently. The consequence overstates the shrinkage: 0.66 is about 58% of the amount effect (1.13), a reduction of about two-fifths, not a halving. Suggested wording: 'which lowers the expectancy effect on amount in that study from about 1.1 to 0.66'.
Unit counts follow from Table 1 df (20 and 36 units) minus the tabulated studies (19 and 33).
Checked against pp. 348, 351 (Table 3 'Conners'), 352 (text 'Connors & Maisto, 1979' for motor performance), 353 (Table 6, 1980) and 359 (Appendix).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low; the six unmet critical items are right. One non-critical domain is generous: item 12 is 'yes', although item 9 judged the bias assessment inadequate, and only two features (deception quality, experimenter blindness) were tested against effect sizes. 'No' would be equally defensible and would not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is defensible: the abstract calls the expectancy effects on deviant social behaviours strong at a mean g of 0.17, and 'no longer necessary' rests on counting non-significant interactions. But point (3) gives only one side. The authors themselves raise the confounded told-placebo/given-alcohol cell and argue on p. 358 that the effects were still separable. The gap text should say so (see missed).

missed: p. 358, left column, 3rd paragraph ('Success of the balanced-placebo design'): the authors accept that the design did not give an unconfounded manipulation of alcohol and expectancy, but argue that it still separated their effects. For no dependent variable in Tables 2-9 did alcohol and expectancy both have significant effects, let alone in the same direction, so they conclude the alcohol effects cannot be attributed to expectancy. This is the authors' answer to the 18-of-20 manipulation-check finding (key finding 16). It should sit beside that finding and in the interpretation gap, because claims citing the 18-of-20 figure (cl_alc_expectancy) draw the opposite inference without it.

Minor: cannot_establish says the review cannot speak to blood-alcohol levels at which a placebo deception cannot be kept up. That limit is the editors' general knowledge; the paper gives no doses and does not discuss it. Label it as the editors' point.
